input.question: if atoms and particles have "rest mass" or "rest mass energy" when they're moving is their mass different? how does the higgs field relate to rest mass?
input.ground_truth: People used to define masses which change based on how the object is moving, but they are ugly and generally an unnecessary concept. These days "mass" and "rest mass" mean the exact same thing. Rest energy is just rest mass times c^(2). The Higgs mechanism gives certain particles some of their (rest) masses in the standard model of particle physics.

Question: if atoms and particles have "rest mass" or "rest mass energy" when they're moving is their mass different? how does the higgs field relate to rest mass?

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a little toy car. When the car isn’t moving, it’s easy to pick up because it’s not very heavy. That’s like the “rest mass” of a tiny particle—it’s how heavy it is when it’s not moving at all.

Now, if you push the toy car and make it zoom around, it becomes harder to stop or catch because it has more energy from moving. The same thing happens with tiny particles: when they move fast, they have extra energy, so they act like they’re heavier—but their “rest mass” (how heavy they are when not moving) doesn’t change.

Now, about the Higgs field: Imagine the whole world is filled with jelly. When you put your toy car into the jelly, the jelly sticks to it and makes it harder to move. The more jelly that sticks, the heavier the car feels, even when it’s not moving. The Higgs field is like this jelly for tiny particles. Some particles get a lot of jelly stuck to them, so they have more “rest mass.” Others get less jelly, so they have less rest mass.

So, the Higgs field helps give particles their rest mass, like jelly helps make your toy car feel heavier!
